content: The evidence supporting the diagnostic accuracy of tests for predicting clinical leprosy is moderate, but the number of studies available is limited. While people are likely to value the main outcome of diagnostic accuracy, there is uncertainty about how this translates into clinical outcomes. Stakeholders may be hesitant to implement laboratory tests with low sensitivity or positive predictive value. Feasibility may be limited to referral centers. The guideline development group (GDG) does not recommend using a test to identify contacts at higher risk of developing leprosy due to the low accuracy of the tests studied. The costs of such tests have not been reviewed, and there are no subgroup or implementation considerations since the current approach does not include testing household contacts for infection. Further research is needed to identify accurate biomarkers for leprosy infection to develop field-appropriate tests. Regarding treatment regimens, the GDG recommends a uniform regimen of three drugs (rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine) for all leprosy patients, with a treatment duration of six months for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy and 12 months for multibacillary (MB) leprosy. Evidence suggests better outcomes with three drugs for PB leprosy, with an estimated 10–14 more patients per 100 achieving good clinical outcomes at one year and 26 more at two years compared to two-drug regimens. However, there is insufficient evidence to shorten the treatment duration for MB leprosy from 12 to six months. A uniform regimen may reduce the impact of misclassification of MB leprosy as PB leprosy. The cost of treatment for PB leprosy increases with three drugs, but simplified logistics and reduced drug management costs may offset this. Implementation may be easier with a uniform regimen, especially at the primary healthcare level, where differentiating between PB and MB leprosy is challenging. Training healthcare workers and developing standardized health education materials are recommended to support adherence to the new treatment guidelines. Monitoring compliance and adverse events through pharmacovigilance is necessary, and further research is needed on tools for bacteriological testing, differentiation of relapse from other conditions, and management of neuritis and reactions. For patients with rifampicin-resistant leprosy, the GDG recommends using at least two second-line drugs (clarithromycin, minocycline, or ofloxacin/levofloxacin/moxifloxacin) plus clofazimine daily for six months, followed by clofazimine and one of these drugs daily for an additional 18 months. If ofloxacin resistance is present, ofloxacin and related drugs should not be used. Despite limited evidence, second-line drugs known to be effective against M. leprae can be incorporated into treatment regimens. Molecular testing for resistance may guide the selection of second-line regimens. Implementation of second-line regimens may be challenging due to higher costs and longer treatment durations. Monitoring resistance trends and collecting data on second-line treatment outcomes are essential. MDT (multidrug therapy) is provided free of charge, but this may not apply to second-line drugs, potentially limiting access for some patients.
